title: Large-Scale Population Genetics Data
subtitle: Genetic databases, bioinformatics and modelling for disease and conservation
subject: Biology
syllabusDotPoints: investigate the use of data analysis from a large-scale collaborative project to identify trends, patterns and relationships, for example: the use of population genetics data in conservation management, population genetics studies used to determine the inheritance of a disease or disorder (ACSBL064, ACSBL073)
Assess the use of genetic databases for the analysis of the prevalence of a genetic disease
Assess the role of data and modelling in developing and using biotechnology
Explain how the founder effect and bottlenecks result in genetic drift
Analyse data on the effect of reduced genetic diversity on the survival of Tasmanian devil populations
inquiryQuestion: Can population genetic patterns be predicted with any accuracy?
lessonIntent: Students can explain how shared genetic databases such as GenBank and EMBL are built and used, model the prevalence of cystic fibrosis carriers with the Hardy Weinberg equation, assess what databases can and cannot show about prevalence, and explain how population genetic data guides Tasmanian devil conservation.
examSkill: Use population data to calculate allele and carrier frequencies, then assess a genetic database or data set by stating its strength and its limits.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome to HSC Science. This is HSC Biology. Today, genetic databases and what population data can tell us. Let's get into it.

scenes.heading: A cancer that spreads by biting
scenes.body: Since the 1990s, devil facial tumour disease has spread between Tasmanian devils as living tumour cells, passed on when they bite.
scenes.callout: Why can't a devil's immune system reject another devil's tumour?
scenes.caption: Devil facial tumour disease spreads as living cancer cells; low genetic diversity is thought to be part of why.

voiceover.text: In the mid nineteen nineties, wildlife researchers in Tasmania started seeing something they'd never seen before. Devils with huge tumours on their faces. It turned out to be a contagious cancer. Living tumour cells pass from one devil to another when they bite each other during fights and feeding. Now, normally an immune system would reject cells from another animal as foreign. So why doesn't a devil reject another devil's tumour? Part of the answer lies in their genes. Devils have very little genetic diversity, especially in their immune genes, so the tumour doesn't look foreign enough. And the only way we know that is by comparing DNA from many animals. Today we'll see how shared genetic databases and population data are used, for human disease like cystic fibrosis and for conservation, and what that data can and can't tell us.

scenes.heading: Genetic databases: a shared library of DNA
scenes.body: Scientists around the world submit DNA sequences to public databases, so everyone can compare against them.

bullets.text: GenBank, run by the NCBI in the United States, stores submitted DNA sequences.
The EMBL Nucleotide Sequence Database in Europe and DDBJ in Japan share data with it daily.
Bioinformatics tools like BLAST search a new sequence against millions of stored ones.

scenes.secondary: Because it combines data from thousands of labs, this is itself a large scale collaborative project. No single lab could build it.
scenes.callout: Many labs submit; everyone can search.
scenes.caption: GenBank, EMBL and DDBJ share submitted sequences daily; tools like BLAST search them.

voiceover.text: So let's start with where all this data lives. When scientists sequence a piece of DNA, they usually submit it to a public database. The best known is GenBank, run by the National Center for Biotechnology Information in the United States. Europe has the EMBL Nucleotide Sequence Database, and Japan has DDBJ, and the three of them exchange their data every day, so a sequence submitted to one turns up in all of them. Then bioinformatics tools do the searching. A tool called BLAST, for example, takes a new sequence and compares it against millions of stored ones in seconds, to find the closest matches. Here's the bigger point. Because it combines data from thousands of labs around the world, this is a genuinely large scale collaborative project in itself. No single lab could ever build it.

scenes.heading: The words you need

bullets.text: Genetic database: a searchable, shared store of DNA sequences or variants.
Bioinformatics: using computing to store, compare and analyse biological data.
Prevalence: the proportion of a population with a condition at a given time.
Bottleneck: a sharp fall in population size that reduces genetic diversity.
Model: a simplified representation, like an equation, used to make predictions.

scenes.callout: A database stores data; a model makes predictions from it.
scenes.caption: Genetic database, bioinformatics, prevalence, bottleneck, model.

voiceover.text: Let's pin down the words. A genetic database is a searchable, shared store of DNA sequences or genetic variants. Bioinformatics is the use of computing to store, compare and analyse biological data like those sequences. Prevalence is the proportion of a population that has a condition at a given time, so for a genetic disease, how common it actually is. A bottleneck is a sharp fall in population size that reduces genetic diversity, because many alleles are lost along with the individuals. And a model is a simplified representation, such as an equation, that we use to make predictions. Notice the difference between the first and the last. A database stores data, while a model uses data to predict something. Let's use a model now.

scenes.heading: Modelling cystic fibrosis carriers
scenes.question: About 1 in 2,500 Australian babies is born with cystic fibrosis, an autosomal recessive condition. Using the Hardy Weinberg equation, estimate the frequency of the CF allele and the proportion of people who are carriers.
scenes.coachNote: Affected babies are homozygous recessive, so their frequency is q². Carriers are heterozygotes, 2pq.
steps: Answer: CF allele frequency ≈ 0.02; about 1 in 25 people are carriers, most of whom don't know it ✓
scenes.caption: q² = 1/2500 gives q = 0.02, p = 0.98, 2pq ≈ 0.039, about 1 in 25 people carry a CF allele.

voiceover.text: Let's use population data and a model together. About one in two thousand five hundred Australian babies is born with cystic fibrosis, which is autosomal recessive. Using the Hardy Weinberg equation, we'll estimate the frequency of the CF allele, and the proportion of carriers. Affected babies have two copies of the recessive allele, so their frequency is q squared. That means q squared equals one divided by two thousand five hundred, which is zero point zero zero zero four. Take the square root, and q, the CF allele frequency, is zero point zero two. Since p plus q equals one, p is zero point nine eight. Carriers are the heterozygotes, two p q, so that's two times zero point nine eight times zero point zero two, which is zero point zero three nine two. That's roughly one person in every twenty five. And that matches what CF organisations report, which tells us the model is a good fit, even though most carriers have no idea.

scenes.heading: A model rests on assumptions
scenes.body: The Hardy Weinberg model assumes an ideal population, so its predictions are estimates, not facts.

bullets.text: It assumes a large population with random mating.
It assumes no selection, migration or new mutations change the allele frequencies.
Real populations only roughly meet these, so treat the answer as an estimate.

scenes.secondary: Modelling is still powerful. It turns one easily measured number, how many babies are affected, into one that's hard to measure, how many people are carriers.
scenes.callout: Good models predict well; they never predict perfectly.
scenes.caption: Hardy Weinberg assumes an ideal population, so carrier estimates are useful approximations.

voiceover.text: Now, the newer syllabus asks you to assess the role of data and modelling, so let's be honest about the model. The Hardy Weinberg equation assumes an ideal population. It has to be large, mating has to be random, and nothing can be changing the allele frequencies, so no selection, no migration in or out, and no new mutations. Real populations only roughly meet those conditions. Australia's population, for instance, is a mix of many ancestries, and the CF allele is much more common in some of them than in others. So the carrier figure is an estimate, not a fact. But look at what the model achieved. It took a number that's easy to measure, how many babies are born with CF, and turned it into one that's very hard to measure, how many healthy people are carriers. That's exactly why modelling matters in biotechnology.

scenes.heading: Can a database measure prevalence?
scenes.body: Sequence databases are excellent for identifying variants, but they are not a random sample of people.

bullets.text: Strength: the CFTR gene and thousands of its variants can be looked up and compared across populations.
Limit: labs submit the sequences they study, so disease variants are overrepresented.
Limit: entries can be duplicated or mislabelled, and well studied populations dominate.

rows: Counting how many people have CF
A random sample of a population

scenes.callout: Great for what a variant is; poor for how common it is.
scenes.caption: Databases identify and compare CFTR variants well but aren't a random sample, so they can't directly give prevalence.

voiceover.text: So here's the assess question. Can GenBank or the EMBL database tell us the prevalence of cystic fibrosis? Let's weigh it up. On the strength side, the full CFTR gene sequence and thousands of its variants are stored there, so researchers can look them up, compare them, and design tests for the common ones, like F508del, which accounts for roughly seven in ten CF alleles worldwide. And because sequences come from many countries, variants can be compared between populations. But here's the limit. These databases hold sequences that labs chose to submit, and labs studying CF tend to sequence people who have it. So disease variants are heavily overrepresented, and simply counting entries would wildly overestimate prevalence. Entries can also be duplicated or mislabelled, and well studied populations dominate. So sequence databases are great for what a variant is, but poor for how common it is. Prevalence needs population data, like newborn screening results.

scenes.heading: Conservation: the Tasmanian devil
scenes.body: Population genetic data showed devils had lost diversity through past bottlenecks, and now guides how they are bred and released.

bullets.text: Past population crashes and isolation on Tasmania left devils with low genetic diversity.
Low diversity in immune genes may help the facial tumour avoid rejection.
The insurance population is bred using genetic data to keep as much diversity as possible.

scenes.secondary: Diversity improves a population's capacity to adapt. It doesn't guarantee survival, which still depends on habitat, disease and other ecological factors.
scenes.callout: Diversity boosts adaptive capacity; it doesn't guarantee survival.
scenes.caption: Genetic data revealed devils' low diversity and now guides breeding to conserve what remains.

voiceover.text: Now back to the devils, because this is population genetics data in conservation. Comparing DNA across many devils showed that the species has very low genetic diversity, the signature of past bottlenecks, when the population crashed, and of long isolation on Tasmania. That matters for two reasons. First, low diversity in immune genes may be part of why the facial tumour isn't rejected. Second, a population with fewer alleles has less raw material to adapt to any new threat. So conservation managers set up an insurance population of disease free devils, and they use genetic data to choose which animals breed, so that as much of the remaining diversity as possible is kept. But watch your wording. Genetic diversity improves a population's capacity to adapt. It doesn't guarantee survival, which still depends on habitat, disease and plenty of other ecological factors.

scenes.heading: Two traps
scenes.body: Trap 1: thinking the reference genome is 'the' human genome. The Human Genome Project built one composite reference from a few donors, and every real person differs from it at millions of positions.
scenes.secondary: Trap 2: assuming a huge dataset removes all uncertainty. Scale strengthens inference, but a database that isn't a random sample stays biased however big it gets, and every model rests on assumptions.
scenes.callout: Bigger isn't unbiased, and a reference isn't a real person.
scenes.caption: The reference genome is a composite; big datasets strengthen inference but keep bias and assumptions.

voiceover.text: Two traps to avoid. Trap one, thinking the reference genome is the human genome, as if there were one correct version. The Human Genome Project produced a single composite reference, built from the DNA of a small number of donors. It represents no one person, and every real genome differs from it at millions of positions. It's a starting map, not a template everyone should match. Trap two, assuming that a huge dataset removes all uncertainty. It doesn't. More data does strengthen inference and helps you detect patterns, but if the data isn't a random sample, it stays biased no matter how big it gets. And every model you run on it rests on assumptions. So a strong answer always states both sides, the strength that scale provides, and the limits that remain.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: A student counts how many CFTR sequences in GenBank carry F508del, and uses that proportion as the prevalence of CF in Australia. Assess this method.
scenes.pausePrompt: Pause and assess it: one strength, then the limits.
answerSteps: Strength: GenBank does store many CFTR sequences, so F508del can be identified and compared.
Limit: labs mostly submit sequences from people with CF, so F508del is overrepresented.
Limit: entries come from many countries, not a random sample of Australians, and some are duplicates.
Better: use population data such as newborn screening results, and model carriers with Hardy Weinberg.
Answer: useful for identifying the variant, but invalid as a measure of Australian prevalence ✓
scenes.caption: Counting GenBank entries overestimates prevalence; use screening data and modelling instead.

voiceover.text: Quick check. A student counts how many CFTR sequences in GenBank carry the F508del variant, and uses that proportion as the prevalence of cystic fibrosis in Australia. Assess this method. Pause and assess it, one strength, then the limits. Right. The strength is real, GenBank does hold many CFTR sequences, so the student can identify F508del and compare it with other variants. But the method has serious problems. Labs mostly submit sequences from people who actually have CF, so the variant will be heavily overrepresented. On top of that, the entries come from many countries, not a random sample of Australians, and some are duplicates. A better approach would use population data, like newborn screening results, and then model the carriers with Hardy Weinberg. So the verdict is, it's useful for identifying the variant, but invalid as a measure of prevalence in Australia.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: GenBank, EMBL and DDBJ share submitted sequences; bioinformatics tools search them.
Hardy Weinberg: affected = q², p + q = 1, carriers = 2pq (CF ≈ 1 in 25).
Models rest on assumptions, so their predictions are estimates.
Sequence databases identify variants well but aren't a random sample, so can't give prevalence.
Devil data showed bottlenecks and low diversity, and now guides breeding to keep diversity.
scenes.finalPrompt: Data or database question? State what the scale lets you see, then the bias or assumption that limits it.
scenes.caption: Five takeaways: shared databases, Hardy Weinberg, model assumptions, database limits, devil conservation.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. Five things to take away. First, GenBank, the EMBL database and DDBJ share submitted DNA sequences every day, and bioinformatics tools like BLAST search them. Second, Hardy Weinberg lets you model a population, with affected individuals as q squared, p plus q equal to one, and carriers as two p q, which for cystic fibrosis is about one in twenty five. Third, every model rests on assumptions, so its predictions are estimates. Fourth, sequence databases are excellent for identifying and comparing variants, but they're not a random sample of people, so they can't give you prevalence directly. And fifth, population data revealed the Tasmanian devil's bottlenecks and low diversity, and it now guides breeding to keep what diversity is left. So on any data question, state what the scale lets you see, then the bias or assumption that limits it.
